title: Counting Rows: Pick the Narrowest Index
description: COUNT(*) over a wide clustered index reads huge rows; a narrow nonclustered index gives the engine far fewer pages to scan. Why it matters: COUNT(*) dashboards and health checks run constantly in production; picking the right index for them is a cheap, high-impact optimization most teams never think about.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson looks at something that feels like it should be instant — counting how many rows are in a table — and explains why it can still be surprisingly expensive, plus how picking the *right* index can make a big difference even though every index technically "works" for this query.

Why does this happen? `COUNT(*)` has no filter to narrow things down — by definition, it has to visit every single row in the table to get an accurate count. There's no way to skip rows when you're counting all of them. But here's the twist: *which* structure it counts through matters a lot, because some structures are physically much smaller than others.

Think of counting people in a stadium two different ways: one where you walk past every single seat checking who's sitting where (carrying a huge folder of everyone's full details as you go), versus one where you just walk past a slim list that only has "seat taken: yes/no" for each seat. Both approaches visit every seat — but the second is much faster because there's far less to read at each stop. A **narrow index** (one with very few columns) is like that slim list: SQL Server can count through it while reading far less data per row than it would counting through the wide clustered index, which carries every single column for every row.

## Scenario
A dashboard runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders` on a 200,000-row table. It feels heavy for something that just returns one number.

## Why it's slow
`COUNT(*)` has to visit **every row once**, but it can do that through *any* index — it doesn't care which columns are there, only how many rows exist. The only structure available here is the **clustered index**, and each row carries a `CHAR(200)` `Filler` column, so the rows are wide and the clustered index spans **thousands of 8 KB pages**. A `Clustered Index Scan` therefore reads them all.

## What to look for
- In the plan: a **Clustered Index Scan** on `Orders`.
- In `STATISTICS IO`: **logical reads** in the thousands just to count rows.

## The concept
Add a **narrow nonclustered index** — say on the 1-byte `Region` column. Every row still appears exactly once in that index, so the count is unchanged, but the index is tiny compared to the wide clustered rows. The optimizer automatically picks the **smallest** index that can answer the query, turning the scan into a far cheaper `Index Scan` and cutting logical reads dramatically.
hints: COUNT(*) can use any index — the optimizer picks the smallest one that covers the query.
The only index here is the clustered index, and the CHAR(200) Filler makes every row wide.
Create a skinny nonclustered index (e.g. on Region) so COUNT(*) scans it instead: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Region ON Orders(Region);
